name: Kabras

tone_statements.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J. 2016. An overview of Kabarasi verb tone. Language 92(3): e134-e191. doi:10.1353/lan.2016.0054
tone_statements.quote: Kabarasi has a tonal system with several properties that are characteristic of Bantu languages (Kisseberth & Odden 2003, Downing 2011, Marlo & Odden 2017), including an underlying contrast between H-toned (/H/) and toneless (/∅/) verb roots. [...] There is evidence for a three-way tonal opposition in Kabarasi: H vs. ∅ vs. L. The primary contrast is between H and ∅; virtually all tonal generalizations for Kabarasi can be stated with reference only to the presence vs. absence of Hs. [...] The tone bearing unit (TBU) is the mora in Kabarasi.
tone_statements.check: quotation from a journal article located by the 2026-09-24 journal search, not yet verified by a second reading
tone_statements.summary: The article describes Kabarasi verb tone from elicitation with one speaker (Kaimosi, Kenya, 2012-2013; recordings reviewed, no acoustic measurement): a lexical /H/ vs. toneless contrast on verb roots, a marginal phonological L, mora as tone-bearing unit, contour tones only on heavy syllables, eight inflectional tonal melodies, Meeussen's rule, doubling, downstep and phrasal H spreading; the word s

tone_statements.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J. 2014. Tone and variation in Idakho and other Luhya varieties. PhD dissertation, Indiana University, Bloomington.
tone_statements.quote: For instance, /H/ verbs in the Near Future ordinarily surface with a H on the initial syllable when the verb is long in both Tiriki (Marlo in prep) and Kabras (18c-d). Both varieties have a rule of Flop, which shifts a singly linked H from the phrase-final syllable to the penult (18c-d). In addition, Kabras has an additional rule, Penultimate Doubling, which spreads a singly linked H from the penult onto the phrase-final syllable

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J., Christopher R. Green & Michael R. Marlo. 2014. Luyia tone melodies. Africana Linguistica 20: 121-143.
sources.note: Open on Persée in principle; surveys Luyia tone systems incl. Kabarasi and may state that Luyia varieties are tonal without stress or note penultimate lengthening.

sources.citation: Mudogo, Maxmillah. 2025. Morpho-phonological adaptation of verb borrowings from English on the vitality of Lukabras language. MA thesis, Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology (MMUST). 122 pp.
sources.note: No placement statement. One generic remark (p. 54) that epenthetic /i/ 'aids in proper word stress and rhythm'. Claims (pp. 59-60) that Lukabras has no long vowels, which conflicts with Ebarb & Marlo's Luyia vowel-length work; treated as unreliable.

sources.citation: Chenenje, Solomon Luvonga. 2024. Phonological basis of mispronunciation in spoken English of Kabarasi people in social setting. Journal of Linguistics, Literature and Language Teaching (JLLLT) 3(2): 60-69. doi:10.37249/jlllt.v3i2.704
sources.note: Explicitly did not treat it: p. 68 'The researcher did not manage to analyze the diacritics, stress, and intonation due to time factors'. Gives a 45-item Kabras wordlist with impressionistic transcriptions (long vowels marked in some penults/antepenults) and a consonant chart; states (p. 63) that per Ebarb 2016 Kabras is undocumented apart from Ebarb's own work.
sources.venue: Journal of Linguistics, Literature and Language Teaching (JLLLT)

sources.citation: Lukania, Valentine Robai. 2024. Morpho-pragmatic analysis of Lukabarasi nominal compounds. MA thesis, MMUST. 119 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress (the only 'stress' hits are in quoted theory about German compounds and a Lexical Phonology diagram). Notes that the final element of a Lukabarasi nominal compound ends in a high tone (compound prosody), i.e. treats the language as tonal.

sources.citation: Osotsi, Eric M. 2020. A systematic reconstruction of the phonology of Proto-Luyia: a comparative analysis. MA thesis, University of Nairobi. 127 pp.
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent; segmental reconstruction from seven Luyia varieties that do not include Kabras (Kabras only named in the classification, p. 12 and p. 14).

sources.citation: Sasala, James Matseshe. 2020. Lexical borrowing in spoken Lukabaras from the Nandi language in Chepsaita Scheme, Uasin Gishu County, Kenya. MA thesis, MMUST. 107 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Five-vowel inventory and phonotactics (no word-final consonants) cited from Mukulo 2016; no suprasegmentals.

sources.citation: Wasitia, James Indimuli. 2005. An investigation into the absence of voiced stop and fricative sounds in Kabarasi. MA dissertation, University of Nairobi, Department of Linguistics and African Languages. 81 pp.
sources.note: Nothing. Consonant inventory and stop/fricative processes only (a full-text search for stress/accent/penult/tone/length: only the word 'accent' inside a quoted statement of Verner's law, p. 8). No suprasegmental section.

sources.citation: Ebarb, Kristopher J. n.d. [c. 2015]. Kabras verb tone and the limitative stem in Bantu. Conference handout ('[HO]'), 'Papers by Kristopher Ebarb', University of Missouri page on Academia.edu (item 12082197). Venue and date of the talk not established.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: (8) Kabras (Kabaras, Kabarasi, Olukabarasi) is conservative variety of Luhya (Luyia). With regard to tone, it is most like Tachoni (Odden 2009) (9) Kabras has many tonal properties that are typical of Bantu languages (Kisseberth & Odden 2003, Downing 2011) a. verbs roots are /H/ or /Ø/ b. privative tonal contrast c. contour tones are generally avoided d. phrase-final Hs are shifted to the penult e. Hs are deleted immediately following another H
sources.locator: p. 2 (printed '2 / 16'), sec. 2 'Overview of Kabras Tonology', items (8)-(9); also p. 6 item (52), p. 7 item (54), p. 7 item (55), p. 15 items (125)-(126)
